top_strength: Hector kept his footing when the customer pushed back hard on the trip fee, and that composure is what saved the booking. Instead of retreating or discounting, he explained the mechanics plainly — "that is going to be a trip fee of $75 and that's just to get our truck out to that location when it's empty" — and when the customer came back skeptical about geography and the word surcharge, Hector answered the real question underneath it by pivoting straight to total cost drivers and confirming there was nothing else hiding: "no, it's just going to be the trip fee and then the hourly rate for the movers." He also volunteered the two-and-a-half hour minimum, the fifteen-minute prorating, included disassembly, and no deposit unprompted, and he handled the Monday discount ask honestly rather than inventing one — "Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday are going to be even cheaper than Sunday, Monday." Ten minutes, a real objection, and a move on the schedule.
coaching_note: Every differentiator that makes Einstein worth the trip fee got left on the table — No Worries coverage, Meet Your Mover, and the On-Time Guarantee were all absent, on the exact call where the customer was openly questioning why he should pay more. When he asked "are there any, any other, any other cost or expense I need to be aware of?", Hector had an open door for the full no-hidden-fees pitch plus the $2,000 damage coverage and instead answered narrowly. Pair that with the missing Save Your Ass speech: this is a five-hour partial move the customer has already been self-hauling for weeks, so "prep before move day shortens the move and lowers your bill, take a carload of the small stuff" would have been welcomed and would directly protect the estimate. One habit to fix first — say the customer's name. Hector used "boss man" twice and Michae's name zero times.
phone_presence_notes: Friendly and unruffled under a pricing objection, with easy closers like "no worries it like, thanks for asking," but the warmth runs on filler — repeated "gotcha, gotcha" and "cool, cool" stand in for real acknowledgment, and the customer's name is never used once.
